ratings.plot: A young man and woman meet on a train in Europe, and wind up spending one evening together in Vienna. Unfortunately, both know that this will probably be their only night together.

verdict.reason: One of Linklater's essential films — a master class in dialogue and intimacy that demands the theater's full attention. Metrograph's restoration gives you the Vienna streets and faces in the clarity they deserve.

movies.title: Days and Nights in the Forest

verdict.reason: Essential Ray on the big screen — this ranks among his finest character studies. The Metrograph restoration reveals the subtle interplay between natural light and psychological insight that makes his camera work irreplaceable.

ratings.plot: A mute gunfighter defends a young widow and a group of outlaws against a gang of bounty killers in the winter of 1898, and a grim, tense struggle unfolds.

verdict.reason: A masterpiece of political western cinema that demands the big screen—Corbucci's visual composition of snow, violence, and moral collapse is devastating in DCP restoration at Metrograph. The mute protagonist forces you to read every frame for meaning, making this rare theatrical showing essential.

ratings.plot: Based on a true story, primarily on a conflict between two youth gangs, a 14-year-old boy's girlfriend conflicts with the head of one gang for an unclear reason, until finally the conflict comes to a violent climax.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip if you can commit to four hours of Edward Yang's masterwork on the big screen. Metrograph is showing a restored DCP of one of cinema's greatest examinations of adolescent violence and moral drift.

ratings.plot: The eldest daughter of a broken and troubled family works to keep the family together and look after her younger siblings, who are slipping into a life of crime.

verdict.reason: A rare New York screening of Hou Hsiao-hsien's essential work on family dissolution and urban struggle. The DCP restoration at Metrograph is the only way to see this 1987 masterpiece theatrically right now.

movies.title: How to Divorce During the War

ratings.plot: Set in Vilnius in 2022, high-flying executive Marija chooses the worst moment to discuss divorce with husband Vytas - one day before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The couple navigates separation amid a refugee crisis.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds emotional clarity in catastrophic timing, using a single marriage to frame the chaos of invasion. Blazevicius shoots Vilnius with the precision of a architect documenting a city about to break.

ratings.plot: When three American doctors-Palestinian, Jewish, and Zoroastrian-enter Gaza to save lives, they find themselves caught between medicine and politics, risking everything to expose the truth.

verdict.reason: A documentary about three doctors working across religious divides in Gaza demands to be seen while the crisis unfolds and the film is in theaters. Poh Si Teng brings journalists' discipline to a story where medicine and witness-bearing become the same act.

ratings.plot: Documentary filmmaker Ross McElwee sets out to make a movie about Union General Sherman's March to the Sea towards the end of the American Civil War, but keeps getting sidetracked by his own love life.

verdict.reason: Watch it; McElwee's digressive, funny ramble about desire and history is a masterclass in personal documentary that rewards the full 157 minutes. The film's structure—where the filmmaker's romantic fumbling constantly derails the Civil War subject—is the whole point, and it only works at full length in a theater full of people willing to laugh at vulnerability.

ratings.plot: Biopic of 1930s Chinese actress Lingyu Ruan.

verdict.reason: Stanley Kwan's 1991 masterpiece about Lingyu Ruan uses fragmented narrative and layered performance to interrogate cinema, stardom, and historical truth itself. Film Forum's repertory screening of this restored print is essential viewing for anyone serious about film history or the power of biographical cinema.

This is Coppola's definitive cut of a masterwork—see it on 35mm at Film Forum before it leaves. The restoration is the best the film has ever looked in a theater, and the venue's projection will not disappoint.

ratings.plot: A group of professors working on a new encyclopedia while living in a Manhattan mansion take in a mouthy nightclub singer who is wanted by the police to help bring down her mob boss lover.

verdict.reason: Hawks' screwball masterpiece belongs on a theater screen, not your couch. Gary Cooper and Barbara Stanwyck generate enough electricity to power the whole city, and the rapid-fire dialogue demands full attention in a room full of people who'll laugh at the same moments you do.

ratings.plot: American professor John Holden arrives in London for a parapsychology conference, only to find himself investigating the mysterious actions of Devil-worshipper Julian Karswell.

verdict.reason: Tourneur's 1957 masterpiece of atmospheric dread belongs on the big screen where its shadow-work and mounting tension hit hardest. The restoration at Lincoln Center is the place to experience this film's command of mood and its rare balance of supernatural terror and intellectual rigor.

ratings.plot: Eight-year-old Ahmed has mistakenly taken his friend Mohammad's notebook. He wants to return it, or else his friend will be expelled from school. The boy determinedly sets out to find Mohammad's home in the neighbouring village.

verdict.reason: Kiarostami's masterwork of moral clarity and childhood urgency demands a theater screen and full attention. The 83-minute runtime moves like a child's quest—every frame of landscape and behavior matters, and the final image will stay with you.

ratings.plot: Ross McElwee explores time and memory through footage of his son Adrian, weaving their shared filmmaking past with an unfinished Hollywood remake of Sherman's March, creating a meditation on loss and documentation.

verdict.reason: Ross McElwee's most personal film in decades deserves the big screen and the full runtime to land its cumulative weight. His essayistic voice—layering memory, family, and the act of filming itself—reaches something rare and necessary here.

ratings.plot: A troubled child summons the courage to help a friendly alien escape from Earth and return to his home planet.

verdict.reason: Essential big screen viewing for one of Spielberg's most emotionally direct films. John Williams' soaring theme and the bicycle chase finale demand theatrical sound and scale.

movies.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp

ratings.plot: A director making a slasher sequel becomes obsessed with casting the original film's 'final girl,' leading both women into psychological and sexual chaos.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun makes films about obsession that burrow under your skin, and this one uses the slasher genre to crack open something genuinely unsettling about desire and power. The 35mm prints at Angelika, AMC 34th Street, and AMC Lincoln Square are the way to see it.

ratings.plot: A bureaucrat in a dystopic society becomes an enemy of the state as he pursues the woman of his dreams.

verdict.reason: Gilliam's masterpiece of baroque dystopian cinema demands the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the intricate production design to full hallucinatory power. At 132 minutes, this is a commitment that pays off—the visual density and structural audacity reward total immersion in a theater.

ratings.plot: Monsieur Hulot curiously wanders around a high-tech Paris, paralleling a trip with a group of American tourists. Meanwhile, a nightclub/restaurant prepares its opening night, but it's still under construction.

verdict.reason: This is one of the great films about modern alienation and you need to see it on 35mm at Metrograph, where the intricate mise-en-scène and geometric comedy actually breathe. Tati built a full city block for this film and shot it in VistaVision; the theatrical frame is not optional.

ratings.plot: Based on Honobu Yonezawa's novel. Set in 16th century Japan, follows Lord Murashige Araki who, besieged in his castle, confronts mysterious crimes and allies with imprisoned strategist Kanbei Kuroda to uncover the truth.

verdict.reason: Kurosawa at his best—a 16th-century mystery that uses historical setting and procedural intrigue to examine power, loyalty, and deception with the precision he brings to every frame. This is the kind of literary adaptation that demands a theater and a patient audience willing to follow a master craftsman through two centuries and multiple layers of doubt.

ratings.plot: A psychopath tries to forcibly persuade a tennis star to agree to his theory that two strangers can get away with murder by submitting to his plan to kill the other's most-hated person.

verdict.reason: This is Hitchcock at his most inventive, playing a malicious game with narrative structure and moral complicity on a scale that still feels dangerous. Anthology's 35mm print restores the compositions and cutting rhythms that make the film's psychological trap work as intended.

ratings.plot: Two teenagers share a profound, magical connection upon discovering they are swapping bodies. Things manage to become even more complicated when the boy and girl decide to meet in person.

verdict.reason: A landmark anime film that justifies the theatrical experience with Shinkai's visual precision and the emotional weight of its body-swap premise earning genuine resonance across two hours. The orchestration of color, movement, and sound design demands a big screen.

ratings.plot: Nelly has just lost her grandmother and is helping her parents clean out her mother's childhood home. She explores the house and the surrounding woods. One day she meets a girl her age building a tree-house.

verdict.reason: Sciamma's shortest film is also her most direct statement about time, memory, and the people we become—see it on the big screen while you can. At 73 minutes, it respects your night and leaves you changed.

ratings.plot: After a bad gambling bet, a schoolteacher is marooned in a town full of crazy, drunk, violent men who threaten to make him just as crazy, drunk, and violent.

verdict.reason: One of the great films about masculine violence and social collapse—see it on the big screen while you can. Metrograph is showing a restored DCP of a 1971 masterpiece that demands theater sound and image to land its full nightmare force.

ratings.plot: Amziah King, beekeeper, musician, and anchor of his community, reunites with former foster daughter Kateri after many years apart, and fends off threats to his honey business.

verdict.reason: Andrew Patterson makes films that feel lived-in and strange in ways most thrillers don't—this one about a beekeeper, musician, and community anchor caught between old bonds and new threats deserves the big screen. The 130-minute runtime serves the character work, not the plot.

ratings.plot: The aging patriarch of an organized crime dynasty transfers control of his clandestine empire to his reluctant son.

verdict.reason: This is essential cinema, and Film Forum's restoration print is the only reason to see it theatrically tonight. Coppola's control of image, sound, and narrative rhythm demands a big screen and dark room.

ratings.plot: Joe and Angela's marriage is on thin ice. When they invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors for a dinner party, the night spirals into unexpected places.

verdict.reason: Wilde directs a sharp ensemble comedy about marriage and desire with real bite. The dinner-party structure gives the film momentum and the cast (particularly the chemistry between leads) finds comedy in genuine awkwardness rather than forced setups.

ratings.plot: This Hong Kong-set crime drama follows the lives of a hitman, hoping to get out of the business, and his elusive female partner.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at peak visual invention deserves the big screen, and this neon-soaked crime film moves with a kinetic energy that streaming kills. Metrograph's DCP presentation restores the chromatic intensity that makes every frame feel like a deliberate painting.

ratings.plot: A girl with few real prospects joins a gang, reinventing herself and gaining a sense of self confidence in the process. However, she soon finds that this new life does not necessarily make her any happier.

verdict.reason: Sciamma captures the texture of female adolescence with visual precision and restraint that most coming-of-age films never achieve. The 4:3 aspect ratio and handheld intimacy at Metrograph demand the theatrical frame.

ratings.plot: 24 hours in the lives of three young men in the French suburbs the day after a violent riot.

verdict.reason: One of the essential films about urban rage and class in cinema, and Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this the right place to see it. Kassovitz's black-and-white cinematography and the unflinching 98-minute sprint through a single day demand the big screen.

ratings.plot: A devout Catholic man's rigid principles are challenged during a one-night stay with Maud, a divorced woman with an outsize personality.

verdict.reason: One of Rohmer's essential moral comedies, built on sharp dialogue and the collision between dogma and desire. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the Parisian interiors and winter light sing in ways the home version cannot match.

ratings.plot: Acclaimed conductor Thibaut has leukemia and needs a bone marrow donor. Learning he was adopted, he finds an older brother, a musician and factory worker. Their reunion sparks a fraternal, musical journey amidst the town's factory...

verdict.reason: A rare French film that balances comedy, drama, and genuine feeling without sentimentality or false notes. Courcol finds humor and humanity in the reunion of two brothers and the music that binds them together.

ratings.plot: The early life and career of Vito Corleone in 1920s New York City is portrayed, while his son, Michael, expands and tightens his grip on the family crime syndicate.

verdict.reason: One of the few sequels that equals its predecessor, and Coppola's parallel narrative structure—cutting between Vito's rise and Michael's consolidation of power—is a masterclass in editing and storytelling that demands a theater. The 202-minute runtime and intricate sound design of the Sicilian sequences and New York crime scenes need the scale and acoustics of a big screen.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan's first epic adaptation demands the big screen, and 70mm is the only way to see it. Catch it in the format he shot it before it leaves theaters.

ratings.plot: A young girl whose father is an ex-convict and whose mother is a junkie finds conforming difficult and seeks comfort in a quirky combination of Elvis and the punk scene.

verdict.reason: Dennis Hopper's only directorial masterpiece—a raw, visionary film about adolescent rage that holds up as cinema, not just as a period artifact. Metrograph's restoration captures the neon-soaked textures and punk fury that made this 1980 outlier unforgettable.

ratings.plot: Assigned to a county-mandated drug court program, Cody Parsons embarks on the tenuous journey toward recovery amidst the opioid epidemic in rural Ohio.

verdict.reason: A sharp-eyed debut about addiction and recovery in rural America that earns its emotional weight without sentimentality. Adam Meeks shoots real locations in Ohio with the precision of a documentarian, letting the landscape and the program itself carry the story.

ratings.plot: While a zombie virus breaks out in South Korea, passengers struggle to survive on the train from Seoul to Busan.

verdict.reason: A restrained zombie film that uses genre mechanics to examine human selfishness under pressure—rare enough to justify the trip. The restoration at IFC Center sharpens the kinetic train-set staging that made this work in the first place.

ratings.plot: Vietnam War's first Black special ops team reunites to share their untold story, revealing hidden military history and exploring whether confronting the past can heal old wounds.

verdict.reason: Watch this. A firsthand account of an erased chapter of military history—the kind of documentary that restores what official channels buried.

ratings.plot: A 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life.

verdict.reason: Matt Johnson captures the reckless heat of a formative summer with sharp comedy and real affection for the kid Bourdain was before he became an icon. The 106-minute runtime moves fast, and Johnson's direction finds both humor and consequence in kitchen chaos without turning the man into a myth.

ratings.plot: A story set in the ACME warehouse, the manufacturer of anything and everything used by the Looney Tunes characters.

verdict.reason: A feature-length Looney Tunes film that works—rare enough to warrant the trip. Dave Green grounds the anarchic slapstick in genuine character stakes, and the animation honors the theatrical legacy without irony or winking.

ratings.plot: A documentary about writer and director Brian De Palma.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone serious about cinema craft and narrative design. Baumbach and Paltrow let De Palma himself do the teaching, breaking down how he builds suspense and composes a frame with the precision of a surgeon.

ratings.plot: Minnesota car salesman Jerry Lundegaard's inept crime falls apart due to his and his henchmen's bungling and the persistent police work of the quite pregnant Marge Gunderson.

verdict.reason: One of the great American crime films — see it on the big screen if you haven't, and again if you have. The Coens' control of tone and Marge Gunderson's performance are gifts that only grow sharper with each viewing.

ratings.plot: Baron "Bear" Bailey breaks a novelty charm to force his co-worker Nikki Freeman to love him, but the supernatural compulsion warps her mind into violent obsession, trapping him in a nightmare he cannot wish away.

verdict.reason: A high-concept supernatural thriller that weaponizes wish-fulfillment into genuine horror, executed with enough craft to justify the runtime. Metrograph's DCP presentation will render the warped visual language of compulsion and psychological unraveling with the clarity it demands.

ratings.plot: When a menace known as the Joker wreaks havoc and chaos on the people of Gotham, Batman, James Gordon and Harvey Dent must work together to put an end to the madness.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Metrograph is showing the 35mm print, which is the only way to see Nolan's compositions as intended.

ratings.plot: After a threat from the tiger Shere Khan forces him to flee the jungle, a man-cub named Mowgli embarks on a journey of self discovery with the help of panther Bagheera and free-spirited bear Baloo.

verdict.reason: Favreau's photorealistic animation remains a technical marvel that demands the theatrical image. Metrograph's 35mm print is the ideal way to see the jungle rendered at this scale and clarity.

movies.title: There Once Was a Singing Blackbird

ratings.plot: A carefree young percussionist roams the streets of Tbilisi, interacting with friends and strangers alike, and tries to avoid responsibilities.

verdict.reason: A rare chance to see Iosseliani's debut in a restored DCP at Metrograph. The film's gentle comedy and kinetic street-level observation of Tbilisi justify the trip for anyone interested in Soviet-era cinema outside the monumental tradition.

ratings.plot: A former San Francisco police detective juggles wrestling with his personal demons and becoming obsessed with the hauntingly beautiful woman he has been hired to trail, who may be deeply disturbed.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's greatest achievements belongs on the big screen, and this 35mm print at Metrograph is the way to experience Hitchcock's command of color, space, and visual obsession. The vertigo effect and San Francisco locations demand theatrical scale to hit their full hypnotic power.

movies.title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown

ratings.plot: A television actress encounters a variety of eccentric characters after embarking on a journey to discover why her lover abruptly left her.

verdict.reason: Essential Almodóvar at peak invention, vital in 35mm. The 88-minute runtime moves like a perfectly wound toy, and Metrograph's print restores the saturated color palette that makes every frame feel like a poster.

ratings.plot: A paranoid, secretive surveillance expert has a crisis of conscience when he suspects that the couple he is spying on will be murdered.

verdict.reason: One of the essential American films about surveillance, guilt, and moral complicity—see it on 35mm while this restoration plays. Coppola's control of image and sound design creates paranoia that feels immediate and physical in a theater.

ratings.plot: Carrie White, a shy, friendless teenage girl who is sheltered by her domineering, religious mother, unleashes her telekinetic powers after being humiliated by her classmates at her senior prom.

verdict.reason: De Palma's debut is essential viewing on a big screen, where the precision of his split-screens and the shower sequence's sustained dread hit hardest. Sissy Spacek's performance captures a vulnerability that makes the final act devastation feel earned rather than exploitative.

ratings.plot: In Detroit, a pop-culture enthusiast steals cocaine from his new wife's pimp and tries to sell it in Hollywood, prompting the mobsters who own the drugs to pursue the couple.

verdict.reason: Tony Scott's greatest film—a pulp romance that moves with genuine velocity and heartbreak. The Metrograph screening gives you the color saturation and kinetic editing that define Scott's visual language.

ratings.plot: A Manhattan insurance clerk tries to rise in his company by letting its executives use his apartment for trysts, but office politics and his own romantic hopes complicate matters.

verdict.reason: One of the essential American comedies, sharp about ambition and loneliness in a way that still lands. Metrograph's 35mm print restores Wilder's compositions to their full sting.

ratings.plot: Two 12-year-olds, who live on an island, fall in love with each other and elope into the wilderness. While people set out on a search mission, a violent storm approaching them catches their attention.

verdict.reason: Anderson's most purely joyful film deserves the big screen, and 94 minutes means no endurance test. The composition, color, and symmetry reward theatrical projection in ways streaming cannot touch.

ratings.plot: When greedy tycoons refuse to return Mothra's egg to the people of Infant Island, they must decide if they are willing to answer Japan's own pleas for help when Godzilla arises near Nagoya.

verdict.reason: This is peak Toho kaiju craft from Honda at his most confident, balancing spectacle with genuine visual wit. The miniature work and suit choreography in the final battle remain thrilling on a big screen, and the film's satirical edge about corporate greed bites harder than most monster movies ever dare.

ratings.plot: Mysterious boat returns to a village 30 years after vanishing. Two men join its crew hoping for better fortune. After one voyage, they find themselves transported back in time, mistaken for the original crew.

verdict.reason: Mark Jenkin's blend of temporal mystery and folk dread rewards full theatrical attention on a big screen. The 114-minute runtime and genre collision demand the kind of immersive darkness a theater provides that streaming cannot.

ratings.plot: Two neighbors form a strong bond after both suspect extramarital activities of their spouses. However, they agree to keep their bond platonic so as not to commit similar wrongs.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's masterpiece deserves the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the chromatic precision that defines his visual language. The film's emotional restraint and compositional density reveal themselves only in a theater.

ratings.plot: A young woman, studying to be a vet, develops a craving for human flesh.

verdict.reason: Ducournau's debut is a rare horror film that earns its extremity through formal precision and genuine artistic vision. Metrograph's DCP presentation showcases the film's composed cinematography and color work, which are essential to how the body horror lands.

ratings.plot: A psychologist is sent to a station orbiting a distant planet in order to discover what has caused the crew to go insane.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for one of cinema's greatest meditations on memory and identity, shot with Tarkovsky's hypnotic command of space and time. Metrograph's DCP restoration honors the film's deliberate pacing and architectural cinematography on a proper screen.

ratings.plot: Anna, a shy 12-year-old girl, is sent to spend time with her aunt and uncle who live in the countryside, where she meets Marnie. The two become best friends. But Anna gradually discovers that Marnie is not quite who she appears to...

verdict.reason: Studio Ghibli's final feature is a delicate ghost story about loneliness and connection that demands the big screen. Yonebayashi's watercolor animation and the Metrograph's DCP projection bring out textures that would dissolve on a small display.

ratings.plot: Wealthy Sunny von Bülow lies brain-dead, husband Claus guilty of attempted murder; but he says he's innocent and hires Alan Dershowitz for his appeal.

verdict.reason: Watch it; Barbet Schroeder's control of tone—oscillating between courtroom procedure and psychological suspense—makes this a rarer kind of legal drama than the genre usually allows. Jeremy Irons' performance as Claus is a masterclass in ambiguity, refusing to tip the film's hand about guilt or innocence in ways that feel earned rather than manipulative.

ratings.plot: A Juilliard-trained violist navigates the New York City freelance classical musician scene, playing gigs that often draw her into the personal lives of strangers, all while living in her oddball family's NYC apartment.

verdict.reason: A sharp, funny film about the precarious life of a working musician in New York that finds real humanity in the gig economy and the people who sustain it. The 78-minute runtime and Hagen's observant direction let the film breathe without overstaying, and the Juilliard violist protagonist grounds the comedy in authentic detail.

ratings.plot: Two kids become spies in attempt to save their ex-spies parents from an evil mastermind. Armed with a bag of high tech gadgets, Carmen and Juni will bravely crisscross the globe on a mission to save their parents and maybe even th...

verdict.reason: Rodriguez's kinetic direction and practical gadgetry hold up better than the dated digital effects, but the 88 minutes move fast enough to work as a fun revival screening. The Alamo venues are the right place to catch it if you want the communal experience without committing to a theatrical restoration that doesn't exist.

ratings.plot: An undercover cop and a mole in the police attempt to identify each other while infiltrating an Irish gang in South Boston.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Scorsese's Boston crime thriller moves with the snap and violence of a director working at full throttle, and the ensemble cast—DiCaprio, Damon, Nicholson, Wahlberg—locks into the material with real edge.

ratings.plot: A lazy, irresponsible young clerk (Sir Tom Courtenay) in provincial Northern England lives in his own fantasy world and makes emotionally immature decisions as he alienates friends and family.

verdict.reason: A essential British New Wave film that holds up as sharp social comedy and genuine character study. Schlesinger's direction gives the fantasy sequences visual wit that makes Billy's escape from provincial life feel both comic and tragic.

ratings.plot: A nerdy florist finds his chance for success and romance with the help of a giant man-eating plant who demands to be fed.

verdict.reason: Go to Alamo Drafthouse; Frank Oz's musical comedy belongs in a theater where the fun can breathe. The songs and Rick Moranis's nervy charm demand a crowd.

ratings.plot: When Sebastian, a pianist, and Mia, an actress, follow their passion and achieve success in their respective fields, they find themselves torn between their love for each other and their careers.

verdict.reason: Chazelle's musical is a rare theatrical experience that demands a big screen and full sound system for its choreography and orchestration. The film's emotional precision in the final act justifies the trip even on a second viewing.

ratings.plot: Ordinary word processor Paul Hackett experiences the worst night of his life after he agrees to visit Marcy, a Soho resident that he met that evening at a coffee shop.

verdict.reason: Scorsese's funniest film is a masterclass in escalating chaos and one of cinema's great fever dreams about the city turning hostile. The newly restored DCP at Metrograph sharpens the neon-soaked Manhattan nightmare that defined 1980s downtown cool.

ratings.plot: Intent on seeing the Cahulawassee River before it's dammed and turned into a lake, outdoor fanatic Lewis Medlock takes his friends on a canoeing trip they'll never forget into the dangerous American back-country.

verdict.reason: One of the great survival films—see it on 35mm at Metrograph, where Boorman's control of landscape and danger plays at full force. The river itself becomes the antagonist, and the print restores details in light and shadow that streaming flattens.

ratings.plot: Post-apocalyptic surrealist black comedy about the landlord of an apartment building who occasionally prepares a delicacy for his odd tenants.

verdict.reason: One of the great debut collaborations between Caro and Jeunet—a fully formed vision of grotesque production design and tonal control that rewards the big screen. Metrograph's DCP is the right way to see the intricate set dressing and the film's deliberately artificial color palette.

ratings.plot: In a dystopian future, a group of students from a Japanese high school are forced by the government to compete in a battle, killing one another until only one is left standing.

verdict.reason: Fukasaku's final film is a savage, formally inventive work that demands the big screen—kinetic editing and visceral sound design collapse the distance between viewer and carnage. This is a rare theatrical revival of a banned-in-many-countries landmark that invented a genre; see it before it vanishes again.

ratings.plot: A forgotten Peter Parker lives alone as a full-time Spider-Man until mounting pressure triggers a dangerous change and a powerful new enemy emerges.

verdict.reason: Destin Daniel Cretton's Spider-Man film arrives with serious directorial intention and a premise that breaks from formula by stranding Peter Parker in isolation. Catch it on IMAX at Village East or AMC Lincoln Square to feel the scale of the action work.

ratings.plot: A cyborg from the future, identical to the one who failed to kill Sarah Connor, must now protect her ten-year-old son John from an even more advanced and powerful cyborg.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing on the biggest screen you can find. Cameron's practical effects work remains unmatched three decades later, and the T-1000's liquid metal transformations demand theatrical scale.

ratings.plot: Two melancholic Hong Kong policemen fall in love: one with a mysterious female underworld figure, the other with a beautiful and ethereal waitress at a late-night restaurant he frequents.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-wai's neon-soaked romance is essential cinema on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation brings the saturated colors and kinetic editing to full life.

ratings.plot: A writer recounts a childhood journey with his friends to find the body of a missing boy.

verdict.reason: One of the best American films about friendship and growing up—see it on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings out the golden-hour cinematography and the texture of small-town Oregon in a way that matters for this film.
A cult horror landmark that demands the big screen—Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see Lon Chaney Jr. and the film's twisted family dynamics with clarity they've never had before.

ratings.plot: Legendary New York poet Ed Saxberger's forgotten works captivate an eccentric group of young creatives, reigniting his artistic passion. Their intrigue intertwines with the bewitching presence of actress Gloria.

verdict.reason: Kent Jones makes films about art and obsession with the clarity of a poet himself, and this one earns its 90 minutes by letting each scene breathe. The Film Forum and Lincoln Center screenings matter because Jones's visual precision and the ensemble's intimacy need a room full of people paying attention.

ratings.plot: When a housewife finds out she is pregnant, she runs out of town looking for freedom to reevaluate her life decisions.

verdict.reason: A restless Coppola film about flight and self-invention, shot on location with real urgency before he became a studio titan. Film Forum is the right place to see a 1969 road movie that refuses easy answers about freedom and obligation.

ratings.plot: Peggy Sue, on the verge of a divorce, faints at her 25th high school reunion, and wakes up to find herself back in 1960, leading her to try to spot and correct the mistakes that led to disappointments and an unhappy marriage.

verdict.reason: Coppola made a genuine time-travel romance that earns its emotional stakes without sentimentality. Film Forum is running it on 35mm, which restores the warmth in Vittorio Storaro's cinematography and makes the 1960s sequences shimmer the way they should.

ratings.plot: A movie sound recordist accidentally records the evidence that proves that a car accident was actually murder and consequently finds himself in danger.

verdict.reason: De Palma's best thriller, a masterwork of paranoid cinema that demands the big screen for its elaborate setpieces and sound design. The climax alone—a meticulously constructed sequence at the Liberty Day parade—justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: When a southern Italian town is rocked by a string of child murders, the police and two urban outcasts search for the culprit amid scapegoating within the superstitious community.

verdict.reason: Fulci's masterwork uses genre machinery to eviscerate mob justice and provincial cruelty with unflinching force. The 35mm print at Alamo Drafthouse is the right way to see a film this visually precise about the anatomy of blame.

ratings.plot: Several women enter a science fiction author's life over the course of a few years, after the author has lost the woman he considers his one true love.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's most visually ambitious film demands a theater screen and Metrograph's DCP restoration lets the neon-soaked production design breathe. The 129-minute runtime tests patience, but the payoff is a rare work of sci-fi romance that uses visual style as narrative itself.

ratings.plot: Five high school students meet in Saturday detention and discover how they have a great deal more in common than they thought.

verdict.reason: A foundational teen film that still lands—Hughes nails the rhythm of dialogue and finds real vulnerability in the ensemble. The 97-minute runtime moves fast enough to avoid the earnestness trap, and the Saturday detention conceit still works as a pressure cooker for honest conversation.

ratings.plot: A cab driver finds himself the hostage of an engaging contract killer as he makes his rounds from hit to hit during one night in Los Angeles.

verdict.reason: Mann's night-vision Los Angeles is a character unto itself, and the cat-and-mouse dialogue between Cruise and Foxx justifies the theatrical investment. Tom Cruise's silver-haired killer is one of cinema's most magnetic villains, and Mann shoots the city with the precision of a heist film.

Klapisch's 1996 debut is a rare theatrical screening of a film that captures the texture of youth and sibling friction with genuine affection. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the grainy, lived-in look that defines the film's intimacy.

ratings.plot: Two pre-adolescent boys both experienced a strange event and later it affects their lives in different ways. One becomes a reckless, sexually adventurous prostitute, while the other retreats into a reclusive fantasy of alien abduc...

verdict.reason: Araki's most disciplined work demands the big screen, and this restoration at IFC Center restores the film's bruised 16mm cinematography to its original clarity. The dual narrative structure—told through fragmented memory and magical thinking—only lands with full force in a theater.

ratings.plot: While doing a thesis about violence, Ángela finds a snuff video where a girl is tortured until death. Soon she discovers that the girl was a former student in her faculty...

verdict.reason: Amenábar's debut is a taut thriller that earns its intellectual premise through genuine suspense and formal craft. The film builds dread through meticulous editing and sound design rather than cheap shocks, making this 1996 Spanish landmark worth seeing on a big screen at Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: Green Beret veteran Rambo takes on a Pacific Northwest sheriff and the National Guard.

verdict.reason: A lean, intelligent action film that works as both pulp and social commentary—see it on a big screen where the Pacific Northwest cinematography and tight editing earn their weight. Stallone's performance is genuinely restrained, and the film earns its final scene in ways the sequels never attempted.

ratings.plot: The Platt family bands together to navigate their new surroundings after a cosmic event transports their suburban neighborhood to someplace unknown.

verdict.reason: David Robert Mitchell builds tension through the mundane, and this cosmic displacement premise gives him room to do what he does best. The 99-minute runtime keeps the premise taut, and IMAX amplifies the disorientation of an entire suburb ripped from reality.

ratings.plot: A young martial artist is caught between respecting his pacifist father's wishes or stopping a group of disrespectful foreigners from stealing precious artifacts.

verdict.reason: Jackie Chan at peak physical comedy—this is essential 90s action cinema that rewards the big screen. The drunken style choreography is intricate enough to demand theatrical clarity, and Chan's willingness to wreck his body for a gag plays best when you can see every impact.

ratings.plot: The legendary Greek hero leads a team of intrepid adventurers in a perilous quest for the legendary Golden Fleece.

verdict.reason: A masterwork of practical effects cinema that demands the big screen—Metrograph's 35mm print restores Harryhausen's stop-motion sequences to their full compositional glory. The skeleton fight alone justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: Two old pals reunite for a camping trip in Oregon's Cascade Mountains.

verdict.reason: Reichardt's most distilled film—76 minutes of genuine unease beneath stillness—plays differently on 35mm than anywhere else. The print at Metrograph restores the grain and color timing that makes the landscape feel as unsettled as the men walking through it.

ratings.plot: After experiencing tragic personal losses, a music professor rents a Seattle mansion, haunted by a slain boy.

verdict.reason: A genuinely unsettling haunted house film that earns its scares through restraint and sound design rather than gore or cheap tricks. The creaking mansion and that water tank are more effective than most horror made in the last decade.

ratings.plot: A gay cabaret owner and his drag queen companion agree to put up a false straight front so that their son can introduce them to his fiancée's right-wing, conservative parents.

verdict.reason: Mike Nichols' timing and ensemble work make this comedy land harder on the big screen than it does at home. Nathan Lane and Robin Williams generate real chemistry, and the physical comedy rewards the theatrical format.

ratings.plot: A day in the life of an unfaithful married couple and their steadily deteriorating relationship.

verdict.reason: One of Antonioni's essential works on marriage and modern alienation deserves a theatrical viewing. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the glacial compositions and long takes hit harder than home viewing allows.

ratings.plot: In 1945, immediately following the end of Second World War, a woman who lives with her two photosensitive children on her darkened old family estate in the Channel Islands becomes convinced that the home is haunted.

verdict.reason: One of the best supernatural thrillers ever made, and Metrograph's DCP restoration gives you the chance to see Amenábar's shadows and silences the way they were designed. The twist lands harder on a big screen with an audience, and the craft—the blocking, the sound design, the slow tightening of dread—demands theatrical commitment.

ratings.plot: Two sloppy actors spend a weekend holiday at an uncle's country cottage.

verdict.reason: One of the funniest British comedies ever made—see it on the big screen where every line lands harder. Metrograph's DCP restoration sharpens the deadpan timing and gives the bleakness of 1980s London the visual weight it deserves.

ratings.plot: What did little Eve see--and how will it haunt her? Husband, father and womanizer, Louis Batiste, is the head of an affluent family, but it's the women who rule this gothic world of secrets, lies and mystic forces.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical return for one of the finest films about family corruption and female perspective in American cinema. Lemmons' command of mood, color, and Southern Gothic atmosphere demands the scale and darkness of a theater screen.

ratings.plot: The ethereally beautiful Vicky recalls her romances with Hao Hao and Jack in the neon-lit clubs of Taipei.

verdict.reason: Hou Hsiao-hsien's fluid camera and neon-soaked Taipei nights are essential on the big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph brings out the chromatic precision that defines this film's visual language.

ratings.plot: In 1938, after his father goes missing while pursuing the Holy Grail, Indiana Jones finds himself up against the Nazis again to stop them from obtaining its powers.

verdict.reason: Spielberg at his most assured—a perfect blend of action, humor, and genuine emotional weight that justifies a theatrical revisit. The father-son dynamic and Sean Connery's performance elevate this above standard adventure fare.

ratings.plot: Two roommates/physical therapists, one a vain woman and the other an awkward teenager, share an increasingly bizarre relationship.

verdict.reason: Altman's most cryptic and visually assured film demands the big screen—a dreamlike mystery that only deepens on repeat viewings. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the pastel production design and spatial compositions that make the psychic entanglement between these women feel inevitable rather than explained.

ratings.plot: A reclusive retired professor is faced with confronting modernity when a group of vulgar youths led by an obnoxious marchesa take up residence in his unused upper residence.

verdict.reason: Visconti's final film is a sharp class collision that rewards the runtime with its glacial, merciless pacing. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings the palette of this Fascist-era meditation into sharp focus.

ratings.plot: A wealthy plantation owner is captivated by a mysterious woman with a shady past.

verdict.reason: Truffaut's best film about desire and deception demands the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the saturated color and composed frames that make his romantic obsessions sing. The two-hour runtime clips along with real propulsion—this is pulp made by a master, not a slow study.

ratings.plot: After a car wreck on Mulholland Drive renders a woman amnesiac, she and a Hollywood-hopeful search for clues and answers across Los Angeles in a twisting venture beyond dreams and reality.

verdict.reason: One of Lynch's essential works demands the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the nocturnal Los Angeles cinematography to its intended depth. The three-hour runtime rewards full attention in a theater built for immersion.

ratings.plot: Filmmaker Jenny Abel explores the life and career of her father Alan Abel, known to many as "the world's greatest hoaxer."

verdict.reason: A daughter's film about her father the legendary prankster is a rare chance to see a singular American eccentric on the big screen at Anthology. Jenny Abel's documentary captures the man behind decades of elaborate hoaxes with intimacy that a smaller screen would diminish.

movies.title: TUCKER: THE MAN AND HIS DREAM

ratings.plot: The story of Preston Tucker, the maverick car designer and his ill-fated challenge to the auto industry with his revolutionary car concept.

verdict.reason: Coppola at full throttle—a visually audacious film about a dreamer destroyed by the machine, shot like a fever dream in Technicolor. Film Forum's 35mm print restores the saturated palette and compositional control that made this a studio-era anomaly in 1988.

ratings.plot: In 1999, a race of she-aliens, the Kilaaks, brainwash Earth's monsters into attacking major cities, prompting a team of astronauts to stop the invaders while the monsters battle Ghidorah.

verdict.reason: The last great Showa-era kaiju spectacle and the most fun monster movie ever made. Honda and Fukuda pack 11 creatures into 88 minutes and let them trash Tokyo with anarchic joy.

ratings.plot: In 1955 New Orleans, small-time private investigator Harry Angel is hired by a man who calls himself Louis Cypher to track down a singer named Johnny Favorite, but the investigation takes an unexpected and somber turn.

verdict.reason: Alan Parker's nastiest work—a descent into corrupt New Orleans that earns every bit of its dread. The film's visual rot and Mickey Rourke's unraveling performance justify the theatrical commitment.

ratings.plot: On a dark, wet night a historic and regal Chinese cinema sees its final film. Together with a small handful of souls they bid "Goodbye, Dragon Inn".

verdict.reason: Tsai Ming-liang's elegiac final night in a movie palace is essential viewing on a theater's big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph honors both the filmmaker's precision and the cinema it mourns.

ratings.plot: The movie is set in chaotic 1920's China, when warlords fought each other for power while Sun Yat-Sen's underground movement tried to establish a democratic republic. The movie tells the story of three young women and two young me...

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui's 1986 action comedy is a rare theatrical screening of a genuine Hong Kong classic that rewards the big screen. The kinetic staging and inventive action choreography were built for cinema, not streaming.

ratings.plot: A scientist in a surrealist society kidnaps children to steal their dreams, hoping that they slow his aging process.

verdict.reason: This is essential Jeunet and Caro at full visual invention—a rare 35mm restoration at Metrograph that demands the big screen. The production design and practical effects are the whole event; streaming flattens what makes this film worth your time.

ratings.plot: The son of the sheik and a dancing girl fall in love, but when he is made to believe she has betrayed him he seeks revenge.

verdict.reason: Valentino's final film is essential silent cinema, and a 68-minute restoration at Film Forum justifies the trip tonight. Fitzmaurice's direction moves faster than most 1920s melodrama, letting the star's physical command carry the revenge plot without the usual theatrical drag.

ratings.plot: Macbeth, the Thane of Glamis, receives a prophecy from a trio of witches that one day he will become King of Scotland. Consumed by ambition and spurred to action by his wife, Macbeth murders his king and takes the throne for himself.

verdict.reason: Kurzel strips the play down to blood and ambition, shooting it like a brutal medieval siege rather than a costume drama. The heavy use of smoke, shadow, and handheld camera work makes the violence feel immediate and the supernatural elements genuinely unsettling on a big screen.

ratings.plot: The Muppets set sail in search of treasure, with Jim Hawkins and Long John Silver.

verdict.reason: A genuinely funny Muppet film that works for both kids and adults, with sharp comedic timing and warm heart. Brian Henson's direction keeps the pace brisk and the jokes land harder than most family movies from the '90s.

ratings.plot: A middle-aged playboy becomes fascinated by the daughter of a private detective who has been hired to entrap him with the wife of a client.

verdict.reason: Wilder's most underrated romantic comedy deserves a theater seat, and this DCP restoration at Metrograph restores the film's visual wit after decades of dim prints. The direction is surgical—every shot places the camera exactly where it needs to be to catch a glance, a hesitation, a lie.

ratings.plot: Follows the lives of heroin addicts who frequent "Needle Park" in New York City.

verdict.reason: A foundational American film about addiction that holds up as urgent social realism. Schatzberg's unflinching 1971 debut captures Needle Park with documentary precision and Al Pacino's first major role carries the weight of a man watching himself disappear.

ratings.plot: A middle-aged artist obsessed with his pretty young assistant, a precocious 12-year-old living in a hotel, and a neurotic lawyer with a possessive mother make up three Gotham tales.
ratings.director: Woody Allen, Francis Ford Coppola, Martin Scorsese

verdict.reason: Worth seeing for Scorsese's virtuoso opening segment alone, which ranks among his most dazzling short work. The anthology format lets you experience three master filmmakers working in miniature, even if Coppola's middle entry drags.

ratings.plot: Absent-minded street thug Rusty James struggles to live up to his legendary older brother's reputation, and longs for the days of gang warfare.

verdict.reason: Coppola at his most formally audacious—a 94-minute sprint of black-and-white expressionism that treats a street-gang story like noir fever dream. Film Forum is showing it, which means you get the print quality this precise, image-obsessed film demands.

ratings.plot: An FBI chemical weapons expert, and a former SAS soldier turned political prisoner, must break into Alcatraz prison when a rogue military group, led by a renegade general, take it over and threaten a nerve gas attack on San Franci...

verdict.reason: Bay's action craft peaks here—the Alcatraz siege moves with precision and genuine stakes, anchored by Cage and Connery at their most charismatic. Catching it on the big screen matters; the scale and editing snap harder than any home version.

ratings.plot: Confused post-teenage virgin Bernard Chanticleer moves to New York City, falls for cold-hearted inscrutable go-go dancer Barbara Darling, then finds true love with a loyal lass.

verdict.reason: Coppola's debut feature is a scrappy, vital work of sixties vitality that deserves a theater. Film Forum is the only place to catch this restoration on the big screen, and the kinetic direction and New York energy don't survive home viewing.

ratings.plot: An intellectually nonconformist friar investigates a series of mysterious deaths in an isolated abbey.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical return of Annaud's baroque medieval thriller at Lincoln Center justifies the trip. Sean Connery's performance and the film's intricate production design reward the two-hour commitment on a big screen.

ratings.plot: A woman grows increasingly fascinated with her body after suffering a disfiguring accident.

verdict.reason: Marina de Van's debut is a fearless work of body horror that deserves the theatrical intensity of Metrograph's screen. The DCP presentation honors the film's unflinching close-ups and the precise craft of a filmmaker working through transgression and self-destruction.

ratings.plot: A love triangle develops between a vampire, her cellist companion, and a gerontologist.

verdict.reason: Tony Scott's feature debut is a visually sumptuous provocation that demands the theater—and this is a 35mm restoration at Metrograph, where the saturated color and precise compositions finally breathe. The film's baroque excess and formal control reward a big screen far more than any home viewing can offer.

ratings.plot: A violent police detective investigates a brutal murder that might involve a manipulative and seductive novelist.

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's pulp thriller remains a masterclass in erotic suspense and visual manipulation, built on Sharon Stone's ice-cold performance and the director's total command of audience seduction. The Alamo screening gives you permission to enjoy it as the lurid, confident entertainment it is rather than apologize for its pleasures.

ratings.plot: A newly-possessed high-school cheerleader turns into a succubus who specializes in killing her male classmates. Can her best friend put an end to the horror?

verdict.reason: Kusama's genre instincts have only sharpened since 2009, and this film's blend of teenage friendship and body horror feels prescient now. Metrograph's DCP restoration gives the neon-soaked cinematography the theatrical clarity it deserves.

Skip the new horror remakes and catch Nobuhiko Obayashi's 1977 masterpiece instead. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, the only way to experience this hallucinogenic, formally wild film about a haunted house that operates on pure visual logic and dream logic rather than plot.

ratings.plot: A slow-burning epic chronicling the emotional journey of four thirty something women in the misty seaside city of Kobe.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip if you can commit to three hours of Hamaguchi's patient, attentive filmmaking about friendship and time. Metrograph's screening rewards the runtime with a proper theatrical space for a film that earns every minute of its duration.

Chantal Akerman's debut is a landmark of feminist cinema and sexual candor that demands the big screen. The 65mm restoration and unbroken takes reveal the formal rigor that makes this film's intimacy so unsettling.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: A rare 35mm screening of a vital documentary about women's labor and dignity that deserves theater sound and image. Metrograph's print is the reason to go tonight instead of waiting for a smaller screen.

ratings.plot: Members of a music band spending summer in the countryside watch the petty dramas play out among the local folks and among themselves.

verdict.reason: A rare Iosseliani restoration at Metrograph is the kind of programming event that justifies the trip. The director's gift for observational comedy and social texture rewards the 95 minutes on a theater screen where the light and sound matter.

ratings.plot: During a 1937 Shanghai bombing, a soldier and a woman meet under a bridge and promise to reunite post-war. 10 years later, she's a singer who helps a country girl. The girl falls for her upstairs neighbor - the same soldier.

verdict.reason: Hark Tsui's romantic comedy is a rare theatrical outing for a charming 1984 film that deserves the big screen. The Metrograph restoration captures the warmth of his direction and the chemistry between leads in a way streaming cannot match.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: This is a restored Coppola film at Film Forum—a rare theatrical event that demands the big screen and pristine print. The restoration itself is the draw here; this is how the film was meant to be seen.

ratings.plot: Francis Ford Coppola's "A-side" to his gang war films and S.E. Hinton adaptations (with RUMBLE FISH being the "B-side") remains one of the defining films of an alternate-Brat Pack and '80s masculinity. Starring a veritable who’s who of ‘80s heroes and heartthrobs – Swayze! Cruise! Lowe! Estevez! – in some of the earliest roles of their careers. A teen gang in rural Oklahoma, the Greasers are perpetually at odds with rival group the Socs. When Greasers’ Ponyboy (C. Thomas Howell) and Johnny (Ralph Macchio) get into a brawl that ends in the accidental death of a Socs member, the boys go on the run. Soon, Ponyboy and Johnny, along with the intense Dallas (Matt Dillon) and their other Greaser buddies, must contend with the consequences of their violent lives.

verdict.reason: Coppola's most vital work about class and masculine rage deserves the big screen, especially in this restored version. The ensemble—Cruise, Swayze, Macchio, Dillon—gives you a direct line to where '80s cinema found its heartbeat, and the composition of violence and adolescent tenderness has only deepened with time.

ratings.plot: Verdi's famous opera is brought to life in this production. The immortal tale of the noble Moor and his beautiful young wife, and of his lieutenant, whose jealousy and lust for power lead him to commit the ultimate treason.

verdict.reason: Zeffirelli's 1986 operatic adaptation demands the theater's sound system and scale—this is not a film to compress at home. Plácido Domingo's Otello and the lush orchestration of Verdi justify the subway ride and ticket price.

ratings.plot: Exploding out of the AGFA vaults as a brand-new 35mm preservation, this 1990s kung fu fantasia from Hong Kong is a breathtaking combination of action, comedy, and cooking.

verdict.reason: A restored 35mm Hong Kong kung fu film from the 1990s mixing action, comedy, and cooking is exactly the kind of repertory find worth leaving home for. The AGFA preservation and theatrical print make this a one-time screening experience.

movies.title: Butthole Surfers: The Hole Truth and Nothing Butt

ratings.plot: A documentary feature about the legendary American punk band Butthole Surfers. The film tells the story of how two accounting students from Trinity College in San Antonio found solidarity in their weirdness, recruited like-minded misfits – queers, weirdos, and nonconformists like naked performance artist/dancer Kathleen Lynch – and embarked on one of the most radical rock journeys of all time. Somehow this band, with a defiantly non-commercial name, ended up as a major influence on acts like Nirvana and even scored a No. 1 hit song. Beyond the band’s story, the film tells the human story of the people behind the band. It gives an intimate look at lead singer Gibby Haynes, guitar wizard Paul Leary, drummers Teresa Nervosa and King Coffey, and bassist Jeff Pinkus – five American originals with incredible personal stories.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone who cares about American punk's weirdest and most influential act. The film captures five originals at the center of a genuinely radical career, told with the kind of intimate access that matters for a band built on refusal to compromise.

ratings.plot: A few years after surviving the last demon apocalypse, Brodie is washed-up, broke, and stuck in small-town purgatory. The long-awaited sequel to Jason Lei Howden's 2015 cult classic promises more gore, more metal, and more head-banging chaos than the original.

verdict.reason: Jason Lei Howden returns with the same anarchic energy and practical gore craft that made the first film a cult favorite. The Alamo Drafthouse is the only place in the city showing this, and it's the perfect venue for a film built on audience noise and communal chaos.

ratings.plot: A young man sees a drunk, cute woman standing too close to the tracks at a metro station in Seoul and pulls her back. She ends up getting him into trouble repeatedly after that, starting on the train.

verdict.reason: Skip the 2008 American remake and catch this Korean original while it's in theaters—a genuinely funny romantic comedy that builds genuine chemistry between two leads across a deliberately shapeless narrative. Jae-young Kwak's direction finds real heart in the chaos, letting moments breathe instead of cutting to the next gag.

movies.title: Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan + "Space Seed"

ratings.plot: "I never took the Kobayashi Maru test until now. What do you think of my solution?" It is 1980. Disappointed with the performance of the decidedly un-STAR WARS-like results of STAR TREK: THE MOTION PICTURE, Paramount executives approach television producer Harve Bennett about taking over the next outing of the Starship Enterprise...but for a far lower budget than the prior film and its special effects extravaganza. To familiarize himself with the series, Bennett watched all 79 episodes of the original series, with one story – season one's "Space Seed" – igniting his imagination. The tale of an antiheroic superhuman named Khan who attempts to take over the Enterprise and who is left with his followers on an Earth-like planet to create their own utopia... well, it begged for a follow-up. Alongside co-writer Jack B. Sowards and young director Nicholas Meyer, Bennett created that follow-up, and set the stage for two more films that, though planned one-by-one, work as a perfect trilogy. An epic revenge tale that also manages to pack in meditations on aging, regret, and how we deal with death, it’s the finest moment in the entire original series canon, and (arguably) one of the greatest science-fiction films ever made.

verdict.reason: A lean, purposeful sequel that justifies itself through character and consequence rather than spectacle. Nicholas Meyer's direction makes this work as genuine drama about mortality and revenge, not just fan service.

movies.title: Star Trek III: The Search for Spock + "Amok Time"

ratings.plot: “My father says that you have been my friend. You came back for me.” Leonard Nimoy stayed with the series to direct this – his first feature and the best of the odd-numbered Treks. The story inverts the theme of the previous film as the Enterprise crew go renegade to help save their friend and heal the afflicted Dr. McCoy.

verdict.reason: Leonard Nimoy's directorial debut is the strongest odd-numbered Trek film and plays best on a theater sound system where the orchestral swells actually land. The pairing with "Amok Time" gives you the full arc of Spock's spiritual and emotional journey in one sitting.

movies.title: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home + "The City on the Edge of Forever"

ratings.plot: The most acclaimed Star Trek adventure of all time with an important message. It’s the 23rd century, and a mysterious alien probe is threatening Earth by evaporating the oceans and destroying the atmosphere. In their frantic attempt to save mankind, Admiral Kirk and his crew must time-travel back to 1986 San Francisco, where they find a world of punk, pizza, and exact-change buses that are as alien to them as anything they have ever encountered in the far-off reaches of the galaxy. William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy return as Kirk and Spock, along with the entire Enterprise crew.

verdict.reason: The best Star Trek film ever made deserves a theatrical viewing, especially paired with one of the finest episodes from the original series. Nimoy's direction nails both comedy and heart, and the 1986 San Francisco sequences remain genuinely funny without ever feeling dated.

movies.title: Star Trek: The Motion Picture - Director's Edition + "The Changeling"

ratings.plot: A decade after its cancelation from NBC, Star Trek made its triumphant return into popular culture with STAR TREK: THE MOTION PICTURE, a bold and expansive vision of the future fit for the silver screen. Years after a promotion to Starfleet Command, Admiral Kirk re-takes the captain's chair of the newly-refit U.S.S. Enterprise after a deadly probe of unknown origin sets its course for Earth. Kirk's crew reunion is short-lived as he immediately clashes with his executive officer, the brash Decker, and contends with his former science officer Spock's mysterious and guarded return. While still a mammoth technical achievement in 1979, Robert Wise's full directorial vision was restored in 2001 in the original Director's Edition. This 2022 version showcases its analog wizardry while also further integrating digital effects work, delivering the most comprehensive version to date.

verdict.reason: This is the definitive theatrical cut of a foundational sci-fi film, now restored with integrated digital effects that honor rather than replace Wise's original analog vision. The 2022 revision justifies a big-screen return for both newcomers and those who've seen the 2001 Director's Edition.

verdict.reason: Wrath of Khan is one of the greatest science-fiction films ever made, and this trilogy represents the high-water mark of the original series—see all three on a big screen while you can. Leonard Nimoy directing The Search for Spock and the tonal range across these three films (revenge tragedy, spiritual resurrection, comedy romp) demand theatrical presentation.

ratings.plot: When Denis Villeneuve hit the US scene with PRISONERS, who could have known he’d eventually be whispering to sand worms and communing with the desert on the biggest cinematic scale imaginable? Now Paul Atreides is an emperor, Chani is back, rebellion is brewing, and the bill for all that power has finally come due. Zendaya caps a truly impressive 2026 in the hugely anticipated finale that demands the biggest screen you can find.

verdict.reason: Villeneuve's desert trilogy demands 70mm; this is the format the film was shot for, and skipping it for a smaller screen defeats the entire point of seeing it tonight. An insider screening at Alamo Drafthouse on that print is the only version worth the subway ride.

ratings.plot: Ridley Scott making a post-apocalyptic movie is all you need to say to get us interested. THE DOG STARS swaps zombie hordes and wasteland spectacle for something quieter and more haunting: a survival story about the people who keep searching for hope after the world has already ended. Jacob Elordi leads an incredible ensemble that includes Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley, Allison Janney, Benedict Wong, and a grizzled-looking Guy Pearce. And yes, there is a dog in THE DOG STARS. His name is Jasper and he’s a very good boy.

verdict.reason: Ridley Scott's post-apocalyptic vision with Josh Brolin and Margaret Qualley deserves a big screen and an audience. The early access and ensemble cast suggest Scott is taking a genuine creative swing, not chasing spectacle.

ratings.plot: Mobilizing the full resources of the Ufa Studios, F.W. Murnau ( Nosferatu , Sunrise ) orchestrated a colossal adaptation of Goethe's FAUST that ranks alongside Fritz Lang's Metropolis as the greatest achievement of the German silent cinema. Gösta Ekman stars as the titular alchemist who, struggling with his faith amidst a devastating plague, is offered the power to cure and the gift of youth...in exchange for his soul. As the diabolical Mephisto, Emil Jannings (The Last Laugh) delivers a performance of operatic scale and intensity, by turns charming, comical, and horrific. This special Kino edition contains the Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau Foundation’s meticulous restoration of the original German version of the film (with unique hand-painted intertitles), as well as a lengthier alternate cut prepared by the Ufa Studios in 1930.

verdict.reason: Murnau's visual command and Jannings's operatic malevolence make this essential silent cinema on the big screen. The Kino restoration preserves hand-painted intertitles and gives you access to both the original German cut and the rare 1930 Ufa version in one screening.

movies.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari w/ Invincible Czars

ratings.plot: It is difficult to imagine precisely what cinema would be without its most influential and memorable titles. THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI in particular stands out as one such notable title in the international canon that in its time and forever thereafter has been heralded as a masterpiece of its craft, the singular model for expressionist, black-and-white filmmaking. A landmark of horror filmmaking, its visual style is often copied or paid homage, and its remarkable twist ending has become all but a modern trope. Its long, haunting shadows and canted, dreamlike production design stay with viewers weeks, months, and years following an initial viewing. The film is credited for introducing the "twist" ending and inspired EDWARD SCISSORHANDS by Tim Burton, THE IMAGINARIUM OF DR. PARNASSUS by Terry Gilliam, and Martin Scorsese's SHUTTER ISLAND, all of which share many striking similarities to CALIGARI. "The first thing everyone notices and best remembers about THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI (1920) is the film's bizarre look. The actors inhabit a jagged landscape of sharp angles and tilted walls and windows, staircases climbing crazy diagonals, trees with spiky leaves, grass that looks like knives. These radical distortions immediately set the film apart from all earlier ones." – Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

verdict.reason: Watch it. A 1920 expressionist landmark that shaped everything that followed, and live music transforms a silent masterpiece into an event.

ratings.plot: In the town of Wisbourg, estate agent Mr. Knock is pleased to receive a commission from Count Orlok to find a house for him. He dispatches his young assistant, Hutter, to Orlok's castle in the far-off Carpathians. He tells Hutter to get him to buy the vacant house just opposite Hutter's own. Hutter arrives at his destination safely and the Count is all too eager to buy the proposed property, especially after he sees a photo of Hutter's pretty young wife Ellen. Hutter soon realizes the evil he's dealing with and is locked away while Orlock makes his way by ship to Wisbourg. As Orlok travels to Wisbourg, plague descends in his wake and the people of Wisbourg begin to sense the coming of evil. Hutter eventually escapes Orlok's castle, determined to return home as quickly as possible, but exhausted and ill, finds himself in hospital. Hutter nonetheless arrives home the same day as Orlok and the townsfolk begin to panic over the increasing number of deaths.

verdict.reason: See this foundational vampire film on the big screen with a live band that earned its reputation by understanding silent cinema's rhythmic hunger. Murnau's visual architecture—shadows as living things, composition as dread—demands theatrical space and the Invincible Czars provide the pulse that transforms viewing into ritual.

ratings.plot: Two-time GRAMMY®-nominated global girl group KATSEYE is coming to cinemas worldwide with a special theatrical release ahead of their third EP, WILD . KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS is a captivating journey into the group's bold new era while celebrating the fans who helped make it possible. Featuring never-before-seen footage, EYEKONS fan videos, and intimate interviews from the group members, the film explores the powerful bond between KATSEYE and their global fandom. A love letter to the EYEKONS who helped build this movement, KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS reveals why this group's story is only just beginning. From the intense pressure of Dream Academy to chart-topping viral success, audiences experience the highs, setbacks, sacrifices, and breakthrough moments that transformed KATSEYE on their path to global pop stardom. Praised by outlets including The New York Times , Vogue , Rolling Stone , and Billboard , KATSEYE has earned acclaim for their relentless dedication to their craft and electrifying live performances. As one of pop's most exciting emerging global acts, the group continues to solidify its place as a worldwide force. From the same team that created Netflix’s POP STAR ACADEMY, KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS is produced by Interscope Films and Boardwalk Pictures, in partnership with HYBE X GEFFEN, and directed by Nadia Hallgren.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a 80-minute promotional vehicle for a music group, not a theatrical film with independent artistic merit. The footage is assembled from fan videos and behind-the-scenes material designed to deepen fandom, not to work as cinema on a big screen.

ratings.plot: Captured live over the course of GHOST’s two sold-out shows in Mexico City last year, 2 BIG TO RIG is the definitive document of the band's unforgettable SKELETOUR WORLD TOUR. Featuring the only pro-shot footage of Papa V Perpetua and his band of Nameless Ghouls from the phone-free SKELETOUR, 2 BIG TO RIG immerses the audience in the GHOST live ritual, including exclusive behind-the-scenes and backstage access. 2 BIG TO RIG was created to share the SKELETOUR experience with the faithful in the territories where staging the show was not logistically feasible – and is a love letter to all those who have shared the GHOST ritual. Shot on 16mm film, GHOST has never looked or sounded better, ripping through material from the band's six albums, including 2025’s global #1 Skeletá as well as non-LP favorites including “Mary On A Cross,” “Kiss the Go-Goat,” and “The Future is a Foreign Land.”

verdict.reason: Skip the trip unless you're committed to the band; this is a live document for the faithful, not a gateway. The 16mm cinematography and phone-free setlist footage have real texture, but you're paying theatrical prices for what amounts to a premium bootleg.

ratings.plot: After a seven-year hiatus following the devastating loss of their beloved bandmate Chester Bennington, Linkin Park's remaining members struggle to find their way forward. Their shared history and enduring friendship, combined with the fresh perspective of two new band members, spark a renewed creative energy that leads them on a transformative journey of artistic reinvention. Following the band from intimate 2022 studio sessions through their explosive From Zero album release and concert in São Paulo, the film UNSHATTER weaves together rare vault footage, electrifying performances from sold-out shows, and candid interviews with band members and fans – capturing the raw, honest story of what it means to start over.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical run unless you need the crowd energy; this is a band documentary that works fine on a screen at home. The 107-minute runtime and concert footage don't demand a theater seat the way a live performance does.

ratings.plot: In 2093, filmmaker Kuve visits Umata to document life after a war banned modern tech. Local filmmaker Mumbi challenges him to create without AI, leading him to discover beauty in life's simple moments.

verdict.reason: A 79-minute animated film about creative constraint has charm, but the low user rating and absence of critical consensus suggest uneven execution. The premise about filmmaking without AI tools is interesting enough for a single screening, though not essential viewing.

movies.title: The Twilight Saga: New Moon Fan Screening

ratings.plot: The supernatural tale of star-crossed lovers continues as the Cullen family flees Forks in order to protect Bella (Kristen Stewart), and the heartbroken high-school senior discovers that vampires aren't the only creatures in town. Realizing that Bella will never be safe as long as he's around, Edward (Robert Pattinson) makes the difficult decision to leave his beloved behind shortly after her 18th birthday. Reeling from her loss, Bella embraces self-destruction after being comforted by Edward's image during a moment of mortal peril. But as heavy-hearted as Bella may be, her friend Jacob (Taylor Lautner) distracts her from her sorrows by helping her renovate a weather-beaten motorbike. When Bella encounters a former adversary with a sizable grudge, she's rescued from harm at the last second by a pack of enormous, ferocious wolves. Subsequently delving into the history of the Quileutes, Bella discovers the secrets of Jacob's tribe while looking forward to a reunion with Edward that may have deadly consequences.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical trip unless you're committed to the communal fan experience at Alamo Drafthouse. The film itself plays better at home, and a 131-minute runtime demands comfort you won't find in a movie theater seat.

ratings.plot: TWILIGHT is an action-packed, modern-day love story between a teen girl and a vampire. Bella Swan (Kristen Stewart) has always been a bit different, never fitting in with the girls at her school. When Bella is sent to live with her father in the rainy little town of Forks, Washington, she doesn’t expect much to change. Then she meets the mysterious and dazzlingly beautiful Edward Cullen (Robert Pattinson), a boy unlike any she’s ever met. Edward is a vampire, but he doesn’t have fangs and his family is unique in that they choose not to drink human blood. Edward has been waiting 90 years for a soul mate, which he finds in Bella. They are soon swept up in a passionate and unorthodox romance. Edward must struggle to resist the primal pull of her scent, which could send him into an uncontrollable frenzy, but what will they do when a clan of new vampires – James (Cam Gigandet), Laurent (Edi Gathegi), and Victoria (Rachelle Lefevre) – come to town and threaten to disrupt their way of life?

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical trip unless you're in the mood for nostalgic communal viewing with fellow fans. The Alamo Drafthouse screenings trade theatrical immersion for crowd energy, which is the only reason to leave home for a film better experienced alone or streaming.

movies.title: The Wrong Girls Best Buds Screening

ratings.plot: It's been a while since we got a good old-fashioned stoner comedy on the big screen. Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat star as codependent best friends scraping by paycheck to paycheck and bong rip to bong rip until a case of mistaken identity sends them into increasingly absurd trouble. Produced by the team behind BLOCKERS, THE WRONG GIRLS also features Seth Rogen and Kumail Nanjiani as the voices of two talking cats, which feels exactly right.

verdict.reason: A lightweight stoner comedy with charm in its cast chemistry, but 100 minutes of mistaken-identity hijinks wears thin fast. The talking cats bit suggests the film knows how to lean into absurdity, which saves it from total disposability—catch it at Alamo Drafthouse if you want low-stakes fun and the social experience of the venue.

movies.title: Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups

ratings.plot: Presented in English Action superstar Yash (K.G.F. franchise, RAMAYANA) delivers a commanding performance in the highly anticipated international thriller TOXIC: A FAIRY TALE FOR GROWN-UPS. Helmed by Sundance award-winning director Geetu Mohandas (MOOTHON, LIAR'S DICE), this high-octane saga delves into the complexities of loyalty, morality, and the struggle for redemption in a world where violence and jealousy reign. Independence has swept across India, but Goa still answers to the Portuguese. In the uneasy years before liberation, in a city where power, betrayal, and violence collide, Raya (Yash) must navigate the complexities of loyalty and morality. Boasting a massive cinematic scale and hard-hitting, stylized action from legendary stunt designer J.J. Perry (JOHN WICK), TOXIC masterfully charts Raya’s rise through deceit and bloodshed to claim the city’s underworld, only to learn that power always demands a price.

ratings.plot: CASTRATION MOVIE is a multi-part postmodern epic by visionary auteur Louise Weard. Circle (Lex Walton) tries to leave a trans separatist cult in New York. CASTRATION MOVIE ANTHOLOGY ii. verdict.reason: A 12-hour postmodern epic from an unproven director demands serious commitment, and Louise Weard has not yet earned that ask. The cast includes several strong young actors and the NYC location shooting matters, but no information exists about whether this sprawling work justifies its runtime or holds focus across two parts.
